books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Sojourner Truth, speech at Akron, Ohio, 1851, as reported by Frances Dana Gage, 1863

stimulus.source_note: Sojourner Truth, speech at the Women’s Rights Convention, Akron, Ohio, 1851, as reported in Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 version. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I have ploughed and planted, and gathered into barns, and no man could head me! And ain’t I a woman? I could work as much and eat as much as a man — when I could get it — and bear the lash as well! And ain’t I a woman?

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Truth’s claim that she could “bear the lash as well” most directly draws on her experience as

options.misconception: Background from the books: mill workers faced long hours in factories, not the lash; Truth speaks of slavery’s punishment, not of factory work.

options.text: a formerly enslaved woman who knew slavery’s punishments.

options.misconception: Background from the books: Truth lectured for abolition and women’s rights; the lash belongs to slavery, not to temperance meetings.

options.text: a senator debating the Compromise of 1850.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Truth never sat in the Senate; she spoke as a formerly enslaved woman, not as a legislator.

rationales.A: Background from the books: mill workers faced long hours in factories, not the lash; Truth speaks of slavery’s punishment, not of factory work.
rationales.B: Only a woman who had lived under slavery could speak of bearing the lash, and Truth turns that suffering into proof of her strength.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Truth lectured for abolition and women’s rights; the lash belongs to slavery, not to temperance meetings.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Truth never sat in the Senate; she spoke as a formerly enslaved woman, not as a legislator.
rationales.general:
1. Hear the claim: she worked as hard as any man and bore the lash as well.
2. Ask where a lash falls: on enslaved people, punished by those who held them.
3. Name the speaker’s ground: a formerly enslaved woman, turning her own past into her argument.
Remember: when a speaker cites her own body as evidence, the argument is her life, not a book.
